system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-01-23 15:11:00 to 2186-01-26 13:47:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for evaluation of chest pressure, shortness of breath, and dizziness after developing symptoms while running errands in the heat. Initial concern for cardiac ischemia was ruled out by normal EKG and negative cardiac enzymes. His symptoms were attributed to dehydration, supported by elevated creatinine and BUN, with improvement following IV fluid rehydration. He also received a scheduled IVIG infusion without adverse reaction, using a different manufacturer and premedication to prevent prior issues. An abdominal X-ray showed nonspecific bowel gas pattern with no obstruction, and he remained stable throughout the admission. All home medications were continued without change. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to maintain hydration, complete outpatient GI follow-up with a second KUB, and continue baseline therapies.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re here today for your scheduled IVIG infusion, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve had trouble with the last two infusions—bad headaches and high blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were switched to a different type called Privigen this time because it’s lower in solutes and may be easier to tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. My allergist thought this one might be better. But I’m still nervous—last time I had chest pressure like a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you very closely. We’ll start the infusion tomorrow morning, and we’ll give you acetaminophen and Benadryl beforehand to help prevent reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And my blood pressure—we’ve been adjusting that lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on valsartan and metoprolol, which we’ll continue. We’ll check your vitals frequently, especially during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also get dizzy when I stand up—orthostatic hypotension. Should I be careful with fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep you on IV fluids as needed. We don’t want you getting dehydrated, especially with your mitochondrial condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My kidney function has been a little off too—last time they said something about acidosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw a mild acidosis on your labs, likely related to dehydration. We’ll keep an eye on your electrolytes and kidney values.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So no changes to my usual meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re continuing everything as is—your aspirin, Plavix, statin, Nexium, all of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want anything messing with my heart stability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching that closely. Your EKG this morning showed sinus bradycardia, but it’s stable and not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to start your IVIG infusion in about an hour. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit anxious, but okay. No dizziness or chest pain so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow with the infusion rate to minimize side effects. We’ve given you Benadryl and Tylenol already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Last time my blood pressure spiked to 170 over 110. I hope this doesn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it every 15 minutes at first. If it starts to rise, we’ll slow the infusion or pause it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about 45 minutes into the infusion. Your blood pressure just went up to 180 systolic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little chest tightness—not like my usual angina, but pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’re slowing the infusion. Your EKG shows no changes, so this isn’t a heart attack. It’s likely a reaction to the IVIG.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. The room also feels like it’s spinning a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from the Benadryl or the blood pressure change. We’ll keep monitoring. Try to stay lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has come down to 150 over 90, and the chest tightness is gone. We’re resuming the infusion at a slower rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel more stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed the infusion. We’ll keep observing you for a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay now—no dizziness or chest pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’m having chest tightness again and shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your oxygen—it’s 98% on room air. Blood pressure is 160 over 95. No EKG changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not hypoxic, but it’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you supplemental oxygen for comfort. This seems like a delayed reaction, but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your symptoms have resolved. We’ll continue to monitor overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your vitals have been stable overnight. We think you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Did the IVIG help overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you received the full dose. It’s important for your immune system. But you did have a hypertensive reaction and chest tightness, so we’ll discuss with your allergist which product works best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I still go back to my regular doctor for a check-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Please follow up with your PCP to monitor your blood pressure. No changes to your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay hydrated, and call if you have chest pain, severe headache, or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your labs—your kidney function is stable, and the mild acidosis has improved with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I’ll keep up with my IV fluids at home as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your allergist may consider lowering the dose or extending the interval between infusions to reduce side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’d prefer fewer side effects even if it means more frequent visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll communicate that. Otherwise, you’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the careful monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—no medication changes, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mitochondrial myopathy and heart disease are still stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good plan. Stay in touch with your team.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for a scheduled IVIG infusion using Privigen, a low osmolar agent, due to prior adverse reactions with other formulations. During the infusion, he developed hypertension with systolic pressure up to 200 and transient chest tightness, which was distinct from his usual anginal symptoms and not associated with EKG changes. He also experienced dizziness and a delayed episode of chest tightness and shortness of breath, which resolved without intervention. His blood pressure was managed by slowing the infusion rate, and no medication changes were made. His mitochondrial myopathy and cardiac conditions remained stable. Mild acidosis and dehydration improved with supportive care. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up on blood pressure and discuss infusion tolerance with his allergist.
